verses.text: Saul was thirty years old when he became king, and he ruled over Israel for forty-two years.

Saul chose three thousand men from Israel. Two thousand were with him at Mikmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and a thousand were with his son Jonathan at Gibeah in Benjamin. He sent the rest of the men back home.
Jonathan attacked the Philistine camp at Geba, and the Philistines heard about it. Then Saul had the trumpet blown all through the land, saying, "Let the Hebrews hear!"
All Israel heard the news: "Saul has attacked the Philistine camp, and now Israel has become hateful to the Philistines." So the people were called to join Saul at Gilgal.
The Philistines gathered to fight Israel with thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and soldiers as many as the sand on the seashore. They went up and camped at Mikmash, east of Beth Aven.
When the Israelites saw that they were in danger and their army was hard pressed, they hid in caves and bushes, among the rocks, and in pits and holes in the ground.
Some Hebrews even crossed the Jordan to the land of Gad and Gilead. Saul stayed at Gilgal, and all the soldiers with him were trembling with fear.
He waited seven days, the time set by Samuel, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and Saul's men began to leave him.
So Saul said, "Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings." And he offered the burnt offering.
Just as he finished offering it, Samuel arrived, and Saul went out to greet him.
"What have you done?" asked Samuel. Saul replied, "When I saw that the men were leaving me, and that you did not come at the set time, and that the Philistines were gathering at Mikmash,
I thought, 'Now the Philistines will come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not asked the LORD for his help.' So I felt I had to offer the burnt offering."
"You have acted foolishly," Samuel said. "You have not kept the command the LORD your God gave you. If you had, he would have made your kingdom over Israel last forever.
But now your kingdom will not last. The LORD has looked for a man after his own heart and has chosen him to lead his people, because you have not kept the LORD's command."
Then Samuel left Gilgal and went up to Gibeah in Benjamin. Saul counted the men who were with him. There were about six hundred.
Saul, his son Jonathan, and the men with them were staying at Geba in Benjamin, while the Philistines camped at Mikmash.
Raiding groups went out from the Philistine camp in three groups. One turned toward Ophrah in the area of Shual,
another toward Beth Horon, and the third toward the border overlooking the Valley of Zeboyim, facing the desert.
Not a single blacksmith could be found in the whole land of Israel, because the Philistines had said, "Otherwise the Hebrews will make swords or spears!"
So all the Israelites had to go down to the Philistines to have their ploughs, hoes, axes and sickles sharpened.
The price was two-thirds of a shekel for sharpening ploughs and hoes, and a third of a shekel for sharpening forks and axes and for fixing ox sticks.
So on the day of the battle, not one of the soldiers with Saul and Jonathan had a sword or spear in his hand. Only Saul and his son Jonathan had them.
Now a group of Philistine soldiers had gone out to the pass at Mikmash.
